newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt cuts import duties five percentage points.
newsitem.headline: Egypt cuts import duties five percentage points.

text.p: The Egyptian government has cut import duties by five percentage points for most consumer goods as part of its programme to liberalise trade.
Customs officers at Cairo airport said they began applying the new rates on Friday morning on passengers arriving from abroad with televisions, refrigerators and other appliances.
The government had said it would reduce the tariffs some time in July and the customs officers said details of the cuts appear in a presidential decree.
But as with the previous round of cuts last September, the government has not publicised them, partly because of their unpopularity with local manufacturers and opposition parties.

The reductions are part of an economic liberalisation programme approved with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). They coincide with preparations for an IMF executive board meeting on Egypt in Washington on July 16.

The board will look at an internal second quarterly report on the Egyptian government's economic performance. No finance is at stake because Egypt does not need it, but approval is important for Egypt's reputation among foreign investors.

The customs officers said the top tariff rate for goods other than luxuries has fallen to 50 percent from 55. The tariff rate on the next band down has fallen to 40 percent from 45 and goods previously charged at 40 percent will now take a 35 percent tariff. Below these bands there are no changes.
"They are fairly modest cuts," said an international economist, who declined to be named.

As in September, vehicles are exempt from the tariff reductions. Car assembly companies are vigorously opposed to cheaper car imports, arguing that the industry is too young to compete at this stage in its development.
The series of duty cuts over the last few years has added greatly to Egypt's import bill but Egyptian exports have not grown to hold the trade deficit in check.
In the first quarter of 1997, the last period for which figures are available, the trade deficit was $2,337 million, compared with $2,122 million in the same period of 1996.

Receipts from exports usually cover only about a third of the cost of imports. Egypt makes up the difference through transfers and service receipts such as remittances from Egyptians abroad, tourism and Suez Canal fees.

IMF executive director Abdel Shakour Shaalan, who represents Egypt and other Arab countries on the IMF board, said in May that the trade deficit was not as serious as it looked. He noted that many of the imports were capital goods for investment.
"The trend towards imports is not worrying as long as it is for growth and as long as this coincides with an increase in exports," he told the government newspaper al-Ahram.
IMF economists argue that in the long run cheaper imports make Egyptian manufacturers more competitive. This will help make them more successful as exporters, they added.
But many sectors of Egyptian public opinion continue to believe in the virtues of import substitution and self-reliance.
The IMF board is also expected to look at the Egyptian government's performance in privatisation, which has continued at a steady but undramatic pace throughout this year.
Shaalan was quoted in May as saying the government had given a commitment to privatise a certain number of large companies by the time of the July meeting. He did not say how many.
Reformers are pressing for a showcase privatisation of a large enterprise to show that the government is really serious about giving up direct control of economic activity.

Earlier in the year officials said they were preparing to privatise one of the big four state retail banks. Youssef Boutros-Ghali, who took over as economy minister this week, told Reuters last month that preparations for a bank privatisation were continuing but he gave no timetable.
